analysis.one_liner: Raises taxes on multinational corporations' offshore profits by closing tax-haven loopholes.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 5 Democrats with 6 total cosponsors, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote and died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 tax law gave U.S. multinational corporations a new low-tax regime on their foreign profits, including a deduction that cut the rate and rules that let companies blend profits earned in zero-tax havens with taxes paid in higher-tax countries. This bill would have rolled that back: it cut the deduction in half, ended the tax-free return on foreign factories and equipment, and required companies' foreign income to be measured country-by-country, so profits parked in tax havens could no longer hide behind taxes paid elsewhere. It died without any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and the Treasury: the bill would have raised revenue by increasing taxes on multinational corporations' foreign profits, and it would have reduced the incentive to shift profits and real investment offshore. Domestic-focused businesses would also face somewhat fairer competition against companies that lower their tax bills by booking profits in tax havens.

how_it_helps.text: The bill cuts the special deduction for foreign income (the Section 250 deduction) from 50% to 37.5% for years before 2026, and to 21.875% after 2025, raising the effective tax rate on multinationals' foreign profits.

It repeals the provision that lets companies earn a tax-free return on the tangible assets (factories, equipment) of their foreign subsidiaries, removing a break that rewards moving real investment abroad.

It requires foreign subsidiary income to be calculated separately for each country where it is earned, and assigns foreign taxes to the country that collected them, so profits booked in zero-tax havens can no longer be blended with taxes paid in high-tax countries to lower the overall bill.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. multinational corporations, which would owe more tax on their foreign profits, and tax-haven jurisdictions plus the offshore accounting industry, which would lose the tax advantage that makes routing profits through low-tax countries profitable.

drawbacks.text: U.S. multinationals argue that taxing foreign profits more heavily puts them at a competitive disadvantage against foreign rivals that face lower home-country taxes on their worldwide income, and could encourage headquarters to move abroad.

Country-by-country calculation adds compliance complexity, and assigning foreign taxes to the country that collected them can still leave companies exposed to paying full U.S. tax on income already heavily taxed abroad in some situations.
The additional revenue is not earmarked for any purpose in the bill; it would flow to general Treasury funds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets real weaknesses in the 2017 tax treatment of foreign profits: the blending rule lets companies shield haven profits with taxes paid elsewhere, and the tangible-asset exemption subsidizes offshoring. The costs fall on multinationals' shareholders, not directly on most households, though defenders of the 2017 law argue higher taxes on foreign income can pressure companies to shift headquarters or investment. On balance the public gains revenue and a fairer tax base at a modest economic-efficiency risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 6, 2018, in the final year of the 115th Congress, and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the referral; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

It was sponsored by Rep. DeFazio with 6 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, in the chamber whose Ways and Means Committee had written the 2017 tax law whose foreign-income provisions the bill would have rewritten.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. multinational corporations kept the lower taxes on foreign profits from the 2017 tax law, and tax-haven jurisdictions kept the profit-routing business; the Treasury forgoes the revenue the bill would have raised.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the tax on multinationals' foreign profits and measure them country-by-country.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.role: Cosponsor, House Ways and Means member
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; as a Ways and Means member he was one of the few positioned to push it in committee.

for.name: 6 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (DeFazio, Doggett, DeLauro, Norton, Schakowsky and one additional cosponsor).

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat unreferred to subcommittee and untouched after its June 6, 2018 referral.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor, leaving the 2017 foreign-income tax provisions untouched.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill; the Ways and Means Committee, chaired by a Republican and author of the 2017 tax law, took no action.

industries.note: The bill raises their tax on foreign profits by halving the Section 250 deduction, taxing the return on foreign tangible assets, and ending country-blending, directly reducing the payoff from the 2017 law's low-tax foreign regime. Their interest in keeping the status quo runs against taxpayers who bear a larger share of the revenue burden.

industries.industry: Tax-haven jurisdictions and offshore profit-routing services
industries.note: Country-by-country calculation with taxes assigned to the country that collected them removes the main mechanics that make booking profits in zero-tax countries profitable, shrinking the offshore accounting and haven-country business. Their gain comes at ordinary taxpayers' expense.

With multinationals' haven-shifting less rewarded, the tax code tilts slightly less against companies that keep operations and profits in the United States. This is a level-playing-field effect, not a direct subsidy.
